summary: Defines the format of Uniform Resource Locators used for designating electronic mail addresses, the mailto: links in web pages. It was replaced by RFC 6068.

eli5.summary: The kind of link that opens your email program with an address already filled in when you click it.

questions: how to pre-fill email subject with a link
encoding special characters in mailto links
subtitle: Web links that open your email program with a message ready to send.

tldr.problem: Web pages need a way to let users easily send emails to a specific address, and senders sometimes want to pre-fill subjects or other message details.
tldr.mechanism: The mailto URL scheme encodes an email address and optional header fields (like subject and body) in a special link format that email programs can understand and turn into draft messages.
tldr.outcome: This extended it from the simple original form with no headers to include subject, CC, BCC, and message body, though client support varies and it has been updated by RFC 6068.

today: RFC 2368 was replaced by RFC 6068, which refines the syntax and clarifies handling of header fields. The mailto scheme is now standardized and widely supported across web browsers and email clients, though the degree of support for optional headers still varies.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The mailto URL scheme is a way to create clickable email links on the web. When you click a mailto link, your email client opens with the recipient address already filled in, ready for you to type and send a message.

RFC 2368 extends the original simple form (from RFC 1738) to allow more functionality. Instead of just specifying an email address, the mailto URL can now include optional message headers like Subject, CC, BCC, and even the message body itself. This lets web pages create pre-filled email drafts for tasks like subscription requests, bug reports, or feedback forms.
sections.eli5: A mailto link is like putting a stamp and address on an envelope and leaving it for you. When you click it, your email program opens with that address already there.

sections.title: URL Syntax and Format
sections.content:
A mailto URL has the form mailto: followed by an email address and optionally a question mark and header fields separated by ampersands. For example, mailto:user@example.com is the simplest form.

To add headers, use a question mark after the address: mailto:user@example.com?subject=Hello&cc=other@example.com. The special header name body specifies the message content. The names and values of headers must be URL-encoded to handle special characters like spaces (encoded as %20) and reserved characters like ampersands.
sections.eli5: The format starts with mailto:, then the address, then a question mark, then options separated by ampersands, like a URL you would type into a web browser.

sections.title: Supported Headers
sections.content:
Any email header can theoretically be included, but email programs treat them differently. The Subject header is the most widely supported and safe to use; it sets the message subject line. The Keywords header provides comma-separated tags. The body header sets the first paragraph of plain text in the message.

Many email programs are cautious about other headers for security reasons. Headers like From, BCC, and Apparently-To can be misused to forge messages or hide recipients. Email clients SHOULD choose to ignore unsafe headers or ask the user before sending a message that includes them.
sections.eli5: Subject and body are safe and work everywhere. Some email programs skip other headers (like From or BCC) to keep you from accidentally sending something you did not mean to.

sections.title: Encoding and Special Characters
sections.content:
Because URL syntax reserves certain characters (like ?, =, and &) for structure, any of these characters that appear in the actual email address, subject, or body must be percent-encoded: a percent sign followed by the character's two-digit hex code. A space is %20; a percent sign itself is %25; a semicolon is %3B.

The RFC 822 standard allows some special characters in email addresses (like percent signs, question marks, and commas) that must also be encoded in a mailto URL. Ampersands in HTML must be written as & to follow HTML rules. Newlines in the message body must be encoded as %0D%0A (carriage return and line feed).
sections.eli5: Special characters like spaces and symbols need to be written in a special code so the email program knows they are part of the message, not part of the URL structure.

sections.title: Security and Safety
sections.content:
The mailto scheme has unusual semantics compared to other URLs: it does not immediately send a message, but only opens a draft in the email client for the user to review and approve. This is important because the URL might contain unexpected or harmful content hidden in encoded form.

An email client MUST show the user the complete pre-filled message—including all headers and body content—before sending, fully decoded so it is readable. The user must explicitly choose to send. Clients should make it clear that this is an email message, not a web page action. Never send anything based on a mailto URL without the user's knowledge and consent. Bad actors could use mailto links with hidden recipients (in BCC), forged sender addresses, or offensive message content.
sections.eli5: Always show the user the full message before sending it, decoded and in plain language. Never send automatically; always ask first.
